units.text: Robolectric lets you run your tests on your workstation, or on your continuous integration environment, in a regular JVM, without an emulator. Because of this, the dexing, packaging, and installing steps aren't necessary, reducing test cycles from minutes to seconds so you can iterate quickly and refactor your code with confidence.

quotes.quote: Robolectric lets you run your tests on your workstation, or on your continuous integration environment, in a regular JVM, without an emulator. Because of this, the dexing, packaging, and installing steps aren't necessary, reducing test cycles from minutes to seconds so you can iterate quickly and refactor your code with confidence.

units.text: When running tests on Java 17 or higher, the JVM requires --add-opens flags so that Robolectric can access internal OpenJDK classes and APIs (java.lang, java.io, jdk.internal.access, etc.). Add the following jvmArgs to your unit test configuration in build.gradle / build.gradle.kts:

quotes.quote: When running tests on Java 17 or higher, the JVM requires --add-opens flags so that Robolectric can access internal OpenJDK classes and APIs (java.lang, java.io, jdk.internal.access, etc.). Add the following jvmArgs to your unit test configuration in build.gradle / build.gradle.kts:

android { testOptions { unitTests.all { it.jvmArgs( "--add-opens=java.base/java.lang=ALL-UNNAMED", "--add-opens=java.base/java.util=ALL-UNNAMED", "--add-opens=java.base/java.io=ALL-UNNAMED", "--add-opens=java.base/java.net=ALL-UNNAMED", "--add-opens=java.base/java.security=ALL-UNNAMED", "--add-opens=java.base/java.text=ALL-UNNAMED", "--add-opens=java.base/jdk.internal.access=ALL-UNNAMED", "--add-opens=java.desktop/java.awt.font=ALL-UNNAMED", "--add-opens=jdk.compiler/com.sun.tools.javac.api=ALL-UNNAMED", ) } } }

units.text: When using Gradle, you can configure the System Properties for unit tests with the `android.testOptions.unitTests.all` block. For example, to override the Maven repository URL and ID to download the runtime dependencies from a repository other than Maven Central:

quotes.quote: When using Gradle, you can configure the System Properties for unit tests with the android.testOptions.unitTests.all block (see here). For example, to override the Maven repository URL and ID to download the runtime dependencies from a repository other than Maven Central:

android { testOptions { unitTests.all { it.systemProperty("robolectric.dependency.repo.url", "https://local-mirror/repo") it.systemProperty("robolectric.dependency.repo.id", "local") // Username and password only needed when the local repository needs account information. it.systemProperty("robolectric.dependency.repo.username", "username") it.systemProperty("robolectric.dependency.repo.password", "password") // Since Robolectric 4.9.1, these are available it.systemProperty("robolectric.dependency.proxy.host", project.findProperty("systemProp.https.proxyHost") ?: System.getenv("ROBOLECTRIC_PROXY_HOST")) it.systemProperty("robolectric.dependency.proxy.port", project.findProperty("systemProp.https.proxyPort") ?: System.getenv("ROBOLECTRIC_PROXY_PORT")) } } }

units.text: Robolectric's native runtime now includes Linux arm64 (aarch64) native libraries, so tests that use native SQLite (the default) and native graphics (`@GraphicsMode(NATIVE)`) can run on Linux arm64 environments, such as GitHub's `ubuntu-24.04-arm` runners, AWS Graviton machines, and arm64 Docker containers on Apple silicon. No configuration is needed.

quotes.quote: Robolectric's native runtime now includes Linux arm64 (aarch64) native libraries, so tests that use native SQLite (the default) and native graphics (@GraphicsMode(NATIVE)) can run on Linux arm64 environments, such as GitHub's ubuntu-24.04-arm runners, AWS Graviton machines, and arm64 Docker containers on Apple silicon
No configuration is needed

units.text: As on Apple silicon, the legacy SQLite mode (`SQLiteMode.Mode.LEGACY`) isn't supported on Linux arm64.

quotes.quote: As on Apple silicon, the legacy SQLite mode (`SQLiteMode.Mode.LEGACY`) isn't supported on Linux arm64.

units.text: Android libcore and OpenJDK have different implementations. Because of that, you may notice different behaviours when running your app on a device or emulator, and running your tests on the JVM with Robolectric.

quotes.quote: Android libcore and OpenJDK have different implementations
Because of that, you may notice different behaviours when running your app on a device or emulator, and running your tests on the JVM with Robolectric.

units.text: Below is an incomplete list of differences you may encounter.

quotes.quote: Below is an incomplete list of differences you may encounter:

units.text: When using `SimpleDateFormat#parse()` to parse a timezone using the `Z` marker, Android supports time zones with a colon (i.e. 08:00), while OpenJDK doesn't (i.e. 0800). To work around this:

quotes.quote: When using SimpleDateFormat#parse() to parse a timezone using the Z marker, Android supports time zones with a colon (i.e. 08:00), while OpenJDK doesn't (i.e. 0800).
To work around this:

units.text: - If your min SDK version is 24 or higher, you can use the `X` marker instead.

quotes.quote: If your min SDK version is 24 or higher, you can use the X marker instead.

units.text: - Use the `java.time` API, with library desugaring enabled.

quotes.quote: Use the java.time API, with library desugaring enabled.

units.text: - Run the corresponding tests using regular Android tests.

quotes.quote: Run the corresponding tests using regular Android tests.

units.text: When using `DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern(String)` to create a formatter displaying a short month name (using the `MMM` pattern), Android will use three-characters names (i.e. Jan), while OpenJDK will use three-characters names followed by a period (i.e. Jan.). In this case, we recommend running the corresponding tests as regular Android tests.

quotes.quote: When using DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern(String) to create a formatter displaying a short month name (using the MMM pattern), Android will use three-characters names (i.e. Jan), while OpenJDK will use three-characters names followed by a period (i.e. Jan.). In this case, we recommend running the corresponding tests as regular Android tests.
